utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I asked the registrar to make a print-out of the updated list of exhibits so that once we have received that, perhaps later today, we can deal with the Poplasen, the Radojko, exhibits. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Savkic and Radojko. Poplasen is not on the agenda at the moment, I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. Mr. Tieger, have we dealt with admission of all of the Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't rise for that purpose. I'm not -- I don't have that information at my finger-tips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just don't recall offhand, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wanted to make a Savkic observation after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm in the position to deal with Savkic. I'm not in the position to deal with Poplasen, as I indicated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing is that for Savkic it's a different matter, we are still waiting for -- and I take it that you'll do that then, give us clarity on which exhibits the Defence is still opposing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you like me to do that now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. And to add whatever you'd like to add as far as reasons are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Having considered the matter, and again I'm grateful to Your Honour's perseverance so far as this is concerned, I do now withdraw our objection to P1056, bearing in mind what we have said about P1055, that would seem sensible. I also no longer oppose the admission of P1057. As I said on the last occasion this matter was aired, I do not oppose the admission of P1059 or P1060; however, we do still maintain our objection for P1065 and P1066. Your Honour, all I say in relation to that is I'd invite the Chamber to look carefully, as I'm sure it will, at the transcript so far as what the witness said about the matters. And I'd invite the Chamber to look at what Mr. Margetts submitted. I repeat what I said on the last occasion. He, we contend, has got it the one way -- the wrong way around. He has in effect in his submissions made a speech about the witness's credibility, and based on that invited the Chamber to admit the documents. That, we contend, is the wrong approach. The Chamber needs to look at what the witness said about the document, whether he accepted, A, the genuineness; and B, the assertions made in the document. He didn't, he refuted the matter absolutely. And in those circumstances we submit they have no probative value and they should not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- on the last occasion that Mr. Josse made his submissions in response to the submissions that we'd made, I did indicate to the Trial Chamber that I wish to make one point of clarification. And in light of the fact that Mr. Josse has repeated that submission today, I would like to make that clarification. To the contrary of Mr. Josse's submission, it could be seen in the submissions we made, we in fact referred to the witness's -- the witness Savkic's affirmation of various documents, his authentication of various documents, and evidence that he gave that corroborated those documents as a basis for their admission. We also referred to other documents that corroborated the substance of the documents as a basis for the Court's determination and as to -- well, both their relevance and their authenticity. We did, in the course of our submissions, refer to the context in which these documents were presented and the context in which the witness made various denials. We consider that to be relevant for the purposes of the Court's consideration as to the probative nature of the documents and also as to the reliability of the witness's comments in relation to them in some regards. But to the contrary of Mr. Josse's submissions, we in fact relied upon the witness's evidence as a basis for the admission of some of these documents. That's all I have to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Margetts, Mr. Josse, his first words were that we should re-read the relevant transcript pages. We'll take time to do that and then we'll come with a ruling. And it's now only about 1065 and 1066.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can confirm that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Anything else procedural, procedurally? Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By way of clarification of an earlier matter, I understand, in fact, the Poplasen exhibits have not been dealt with yet so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- I'm not proposing we do so however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked the registrar to give the list -- last pages of the list so that we can go through them more quickly than to have everything being read out, and if the parties have that list then in front of them that goes quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And finally, I want to identify one small problem and also propose one solution to that. With respect to the Radojko exhibits, tab 48 did not receive a number, but I understand that the number-- the exhibit number, 1108, is available because it was vacated for another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Registrar, would tab --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 48, Your Honours, was the excerpt of the transcript of the 20th Assembly Session would be given Prosecution Exhibit number P1108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I further observe that we have not fully resolved yet the numbering of some of the complex 64A exhibits, and therefore -- although it's a kind of an urgency, if we are dealing with any new exhibits at this moment, even if they are already in evidence, they will be assigned new numbers. It's not the way I would prefer to do it, but in the present circumstances it's a safer way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was very helpfully passed on to me this morning and I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, one further matter, and that is Mr. Josse and I have had discussions in relation to the 65 ter in respect of the current witness. And whilst we, the Prosecution, does not know what topics Mr. Josse intends to deal with today, we are aware from the various documents that he's referred to us that it's highly likely that this witness's evidence will deal with topics which were not the subject of the 65 ter. Presently it's not our intention to intervene if we don't need to, but what we would like to do is reserve our position in relation to that at the conclusion of the evidence in chief assess what position we are in with regard to whether or not we can proceed with the cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's on the record, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, shortly prior to the -- Your Honour coming into court, Mr. Krajisnik indicated to me that at some point today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that at a later stage he would like to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He would. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I forget it, which I hope I will not, then please remind me of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Krajisnik will make sure I remind you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lakic. Please be seated. Mr. Lakic, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, and I would also -- would like to ask you to very carefully listen to the question and to focus your answer on what Mr. Josse asks you. So, for example, if he would ask you: Have you come by car? Then he might not be interested in the colour of the car but just on whether you came by car, by tram, or by train, or by bus. So try to focus your answers on what is specifically asked you. If Mr. Josse would like to know more, as the make of the car, the colour of the car, he'll certainly ask you. Yes? Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, I want to start this afternoon by asking you to have a look at tab 2 in the binder, which is a document that you have brought to The Hague. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And regrettably we don't have a translation for this document, but I'd also like you to have a look at this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I have plenty of copies here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And this document is translated and I'm grateful to my learned friends' assistance in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I find two documents under tab 2. Is that correct, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, that may be may be right for some -- Mr. Margetts and I had a little discussion about this, this morning. Unfortunately, my bundle, for some reason, is defective and only has one document in it. Could I have a look at the registrar's copy for a minute, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, bearing in mind the bundle I have just seen, I don't need to hand out this second document. Because in Your Honours' copy we can see a document that says the director of the federal commodity reserves. On the back of that is, what I assume, the B/C/S version of that document. And then is the document on the opposite side that's addressed to the Automoto organisation in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- the witness has brought with him and doesn't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I see at this moment. Let's proceed, and it's not a very lengthy document so finally we might be able to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact, I think, Mr. Lakic, you brought both of these documents with you. It transpires that one of them is in evidence in this case and one is not. But you brought them both with you; that's all I want to ascertain from you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as I've explained --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- and I'll explain again --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- the one to the federal commodity organisation has been translated, but the other one, to the automobile association in Belgrade, has not been. It's similar, but perhaps you could read out at least the first paragraph and we can get an idea of what that's about. The automobile document, please read out the first paragraph slowly.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina find themselves in a very difficult material position, as they have been drawn into a war. The whirlwind of war has engulfed most of the places where Serbs live. This misfortune is even greater because of the very adverse weather conditions, the cold, rain, and snow."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I should have asked you. Could you read out to whom this document is addressed.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Automobile Association of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- sorry, Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we can see that both documents were sent by Mr. Djeric. So the one that you have just read from is an appeal for motor cars. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why -- I appreciate these were sent before you joined the government, but do you know why they were sent?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before I came, but the situation was such that there weren't any vehicles so we're asking the automobile association to give the government within the scope of their possibilities a certain number of automobiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why, as you understand it, did the government feel it necessary to make the appeal for automobiles to the automobile association and for goods from the federal commodity reserve?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the motive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you became involved in the government, was the government short of motor cars?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so why did you bring these documents to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I collected all documents that I could use as a witness; among them, I found this document, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what were you hoping to demonstrate by producing these?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was hoping to demonstrate was that the government did not have automobiles, did not have any vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is that the federal commodity reserve document is P64A, binder 25, footnote 718. And I'm grateful to Mr. Margetts for helping me so far as that's concerned. The other document, as far as I'm aware, has not previously been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it should be assigned provisionally an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D147, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D147, awaiting ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the difficulties we are facing with P64A, Mr. Josse, even if it would be a double number, the federal commodity reserves document would then get -- Mr. Registrar, I take it D148?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, D148.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. D148.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see how the system's going to work now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we may have doubles now, but at least it avoids any further confusion. By the way, Mr. Josse, it was nice that you asked the witness to read the first lines there. They are literally the same as the other document, so we had the translation already, including this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked him to read it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All those documents are not identical --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Document is not identical, but the part you asked him to read is exactly identical to the first four lines [sic] up to this now of the other document. Yes, please proceed. I must correct myself, it's not literally, although the translation is the same -- has the same few words different. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like you to have a look at tab 4, please. This is another document that you brought with you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you -- we can see it's a government document dated the 7th of May, 1992. It's signed by yourself as secretary of the government. Could you read out the body of the document slowly.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the basis of the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mrs. Rabija Subic has been appointed coordinator in the Ministry of Health, Labour, and Social Welfare, and -- for Families, and she is authorised to coordinate activities for collecting humanitarian and other forms of aid for the needs of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We kindly ask that all necessary assistance be given to the mentioned person in view of the duties entrusted to her by the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, a few questions on this. First of all, did you sign many documents of this type when you became secretary of the government?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why did you sign this particular document then?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was ordered to do so by the president of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why didn't the president or the Prime Minister of the government do that himself?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And to whom was this document sent?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the document was sent to all those willing to provide some humanitarian assistance to the government or to the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the person appointed to this job, Ms. Subic, who was she?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who she is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you ever met her?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That same evening when I drafted this document, the Prime Minister was present there as well as some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. Did you at any stage meet Ms. Subic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the only time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you met her that day?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know what her ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what her ethnicity was, but judging by her name I could venture a guess that she was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And have you any idea as to how she got on coordinating these humanitarian supplies on behalf of the government?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the document have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D150, Your Honours -- D149. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We saw yesterday, Mr. Lakic, that in -- that on the 27th of April of 1992 you were appointed secretary to the government. How soon thereafter did you commence attending sessions of the government?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This question presumes a fact which is not in evidence. The fact of a formal appointment does not shed light to the extent Mr. Josse suggests in relation to that subject --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what would happen -- is it your concern that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to be brief, it's a leading question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah, it's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what harm could be done on this inquest? And let's first ask the witness: Did you attend any sessions of the government once you were appointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Margetts, usually secretaries of bodies attend meetings of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could develop my submissions if the witness removed his earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think at this moment -- the matter has been resolved, I take it, now, for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, the matter has not been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Lakic, could you take off your earphones for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe we could ask him first whether or not he understands English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you understand English, Mr. Lakic? No, no, he seems not to understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm satisfied that that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't understand English. Yes. He proved it right away. Yes, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 65 ter that was provided to us suggested that prior to the formal appointment, certain duties had been undertaken; furthermore, certain materials that we're looking at suggest that possibly prior to the formal appointment certain duties had been undertaken. So we would like that to be established in a non-leading fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I now understand. Your concern is not whether he attended but whether he started only to attend once he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, that seems to be -- I -- I take it that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, my learned friend can ask that question. I mean, the question I asked was a leading question. It was a leading question because it's all over the documents, the attending countless sessions. My learned friend wants to inquire what went on earlier, then he can do that; I don't intend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but he objected against leading at this point because it would put him in a situation that he might understand you to suggest to him that he only started attending once he was appointed and that he did not before; and therefore, he objects against leading. But let's -- let's keep matters as simple as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If Your Honour would like to ask a question, then I have no difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I -- Mr. Margetts, that's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I could refer my learned friend to the 65 ter that he provided to the Prosecution, wherein a date of commencement was set out, that being 16 or 17 April, 1992, and possibly if my learned friend referred to that information, he could base his questions on that information he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, I suggest your question was leading, that you explore the matter in a non-leading way to find out if the witness at any early stage attended those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The 65 ter was wrong. He told me that. It's not for me to give evidence, but that's why I dealt with it like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 65 ter was wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, the 65 ter was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you informed Mr. Margetts of this fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, if the 65 ter is wrong and Mr. Margetts relies on it, then I think it's a better idea to correct any mistake in the 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed, and nevertheless I think it's fair, since you have not informed Mr. Margetts that in a non-leading -- I'll do it myself. Could the witness please put his earphones. That's not -- otherwise procedural issues become more important than the substance. Mr. Lakic, before you were appointed secretary of the government, did you attend meetings of governmental bodies or even the government itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not. I wasn't present during the meetings of the government or of the counsel because on certain occasions it was a joint session by the government and the counsel. Prior to my taking up these duties, I was working with the municipal misdemeanour court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I have a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, could the witness have a look, please, at this document. I will try my very best not to lead on matters which I might otherwise have been more contentious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We do not know yet what is presented to the witness at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is for the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's for the ELMO, yes. This is for the witness and that's for the ELMO. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A name appears there at the bottom. Whose name is it, please? I've been told not to lead you, you see, Mr. Lakic, so I'm going to ask you non-leading questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Josse, let's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's your name, isn't it, as well as Mr. Djeric's?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, the -- presumably the only way you could ascertain whether that was the first set of minutes that you in fact signed is by looking at all the previous minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, what's the document in front of the witness. I see now on the ELMO, I see six lines of a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The 13th Session of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Dated the 23rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right, isn't it, sir? Mr. Lakic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the name of Velibor Ostojic. I didn't used to know him personally, but I heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, I'm going to stop you. In the English translation we have got, on page 2 there are two names at the bottom, secretary to the government, Nedeljko Lakic; government President, Professor Dr. Branko Djeric. Do those two names appear in the original?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know whether that was a first set of minutes that you signed?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was that the first meeting that you attended or can't you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea why those were the first set of minutes that you signed?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all likelihood, that was at the moment when the Council for National Security had been split or separated and also one of the first instances of the official sessions of the newly appointed government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the Court's reference I can indicate that the government minutes of 23 May, 1992, have Exhibit Number P529 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Tab 107. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does Your Honour want those to have a new number? That's the only reference I intend to make to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is team-work, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think this one doesn't need a number. It's well accessible for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll have those documents back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the point that you became -- well, at the point that you began to sign these minutes, how were the minutes taken at the relevant meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I started signing these minutes, those were one of the first steps made by the new government, and it was the first time that the government appeared as an independent, executive body, having the Prime Minister and the ministers present at this session. I wanted to mention, though, that I was not a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I was trying to ask you about, Mr. Lakic, was minute-taking. I don't think we need to spend very long on this, but the physical act of minute-taking, how was that performed at the meetings? Did you do it yourself? Did someone help you? Were the sessions recorded?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time there were no recordings made of the sessions. I worked on the basis of the minutes kept by myself to a large extent. The lady I mentioned yesterday was the only one with a university degree, and in the initial phases she still wasn't with the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to show you the minutes of the 5th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that that's P583, tab 16?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And again, I hope I'll be permitted to lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: These were the first minutes in which the names of the attendees was recorded. Whose idea was it to record the names of those attending the meetings?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea was mine and that of the Prime Minister so that, first of all, we would know who the members of the government were and who was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And thereafter that was done for most, if not every meeting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I have that back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to now concentrate, please, on discussions at various meetings of prisoners and the such-like. It might be best, first of all, that ask you to look at tab 5.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are two separate documents in tab 5, both dated the 15th of May, both from Mr. Djeric. Can you confirm that these two --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may stop Mr. Josse there. He may have misspoken as to the authorship of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I did. Thank you very much. I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The first document we see that is an order that the Sokolac Crisis Staff is from Dr. Djeric. The second document, which is a note to the Crisis Staff of Ilijas, is signed by you. Are these two documents related in any way?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you explain in what way they are related.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prime Minister issued an order that a number of detainees who, if I remember correctly were from Bratunac, were to be transported in a safe manner to the territory of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, to the territory that was not under the control of the RS. In carrying out of that order - and I can't recall precisely what the exact number of the detainees concerned was - I tried to secure transportation from two municipalities, those of Sokolac and Ilijas, in order to be able to implement the order of the Prime Minister and for those people to be transported to the territory of the Federation of B & H.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why did these people need to be transported at all?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people were detainees mainly and they had to be transported for safety reasons and in such a way that their safety was -- would not -- was not jeopardised in any way in their process of being transported through the territory of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know why they were being detained?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why did this operation involve you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Prime Minister ordered that I carry out this task, and I was the then-secretary to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The document that you signed was designed, presumably, for the Crisis Staff at Ilijas. How was it going to get to the Crisis Staff at Ilijas, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reached the Crisis Staff of Ilijas because it was arranged for those people to be transported to the territory of Visoko, and the municipality of Ilijas is adjacent to the municipality of Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That doesn't explain how the document was going to get to the Crisis Staff. I could ask you a leading question, but I suspect that I'd be stopped from doing that. How, physically, was the document meant to get to the Crisis Staff at Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view and in my knowledge, the telephone lines were cut off and I wasn't sure whether that would eventually reach the Crisis Staff. So we entrusted the document to a person who carried it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And was the person who carried it there with the detainees or did he go to Ilijas on his own?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was one of the policemen. I can't recall his name, but he was within the security detail of the convoy and he was carrying that letter to the Crisis Staff of Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We see that you have said: "Please destroy that approval the moment when the prisoners leave Ilijas municipality." Why did you write that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote that because we were in the state of war and for security reasons, to make it safer for the security detail as well as for those who were being transported to the territory of Visoko municipality. The war was ongoing and the concern was that of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea how it is in those circumstances that the document still exists?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that this document is in dispute. It doesn't -- it simply confirms certain things, and this was with the interest of guaranteeing the safety of the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Both documents, Your Honour, have numbers. I don't know if Your Honour wishes them to have new numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I don't think we need new numbers for these documents. But could I ask the witness: In -- how could the -- how could the existence of this document affect the security of anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It concerned the safety of all those on the convoy, the detainees and the security detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but once they left the municipality, how could that harm the safety of the -- of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In all likelihood, that concerned the people who were securing the transport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still do not understand. Does it -- how could they be affected by the existence of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an order for the organs of the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say the police. At that moment, at that time, about 50 people from Pale got killed in fighting with the members of the units of the Territorial Defence of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still don't understand. I mean, people are escorting a large group of detainees, so it seems not to be a great secret that they are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- accompanying detainees. Once they have them -- delivered them somewhere, then what does this document say? Nothing, apart from that there had been a transport and they had been escorted and that the Crisis Staff of Ilijas was to cooperate. How could that affect security of -- again, of whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, there was a war going on, and this was done just in case so that it would be known that they -- these people were not transported through the territory of the municipality of Pale and Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did -- they were or they were not transported? Your answer is not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were transported and safely so to the territory of the municipality of Visoko. And there were no excesses on the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but during the transport the document still existed, isn't it, because it was to be destroyed once the prisoners leave Ilijas municipality, not when they were still there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably somebody didn't do that, although it was their duty to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not an answer to my question. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I have a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look, please, at tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if I could address this question, obviously, to the Trial Chamber and ultimately to Mr. Josse. In the materials we were presented with yesterday, a particular translation of this document was presented and I've alerted Mr. Josse to the fact that that's an erroneous translation, that's the one headed "draft translation" on the first page, L0101953, and I've supplied to Mr. Josse the corrected translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I've got plenty of copies here and I'm grateful to Mr. Margetts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before we continue, the two documents were said would not need a new number, the two 15th of May documents are tab 123 and tab 124. I take it from P exhibit 583. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you seen this report before?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In what circumstances have you seen this report?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the government discussed the issue of refugees and detained persons and set up a central commission to ascertain what the situation was in the camps, in the collection camps, and then information was supposed to be presented to the government. On the basis of that information, the president of the central commission passed this order related to the treatment of refugees and displaced persons in these centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look, please, at the 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, do we have already a number for tab 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Tab 6, the order dated 6th June, 1992, was first presented as Exhibit P435; subsequently it also gained an additional number, P583, Trbojevic, tab 75.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And was that with the better, new translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a -- well, I'll put it -- quite frankly, this is an embarrassing situation. The P435 was presented with the correct translation, and in dealing with the document on the second occasion when it gained the second number, the wrong translation was dealt with in Court I believe. There is a discernible difference between the two translations, if Your Honour would wish to compare them, and the difference is the fourth paragraph on the correct translation is missing from the defective translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Margetts, you're invited to present to the registrar a replacement with the right correction of P583, tab 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we'll do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we'll work --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can do that now, I've got one here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've all got one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I've got it because Mr. Margetts was good enough to send it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's proceed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to have a look, please, at the minutes of the 24th government session, 9th of June, 1992, and it's first page in English that needs to go on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We see item number 1 on the agenda of this particular meeting is the fact that the government has supported the order of the Central Committee for the Exchange of Prisoners and acknowledged the letter of correspondence in the presence of the Central Committee for the Exchange of the Prisoners. Is this a reference to the document?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The witness said something I didn't get a translation of.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, Mr. Lakic, because the interpreters could not hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, you said something a moment ago, one or two words, what was it you just said, please?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is: Is this a reference to item number 1 in the report I've just asked you to look at?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And if we turn to page 2 in the English, you've got it there and the -- well, I think the second page in the original, Mr. Lakic. We see what the government stance is in relation to the treatment of exchange of prisoners. What was your role in the matters described in that document? The minutes I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My role was to formulate the positions of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we can see the role -- the stance the government was taking in relation to this matter. Were these -- was the government stance put into effect?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government regularly monitored the situation in these collection centres and camps, and the position was to carry out an exchange -- or rather, to first release all those civilians who had not participated in war operations, to provide proper sanitary conditions for them, to observe the provisions of humanitarian law. Then persons in camps were supposed to be given food regularly or -- actually, they were allowed to have their families bring food in. Women were given special treatment by way of appropriate sanitary technical conditions, apart from those provided for the men. Further on, to have exchanges carried out as soon as possible, exchanges of detainees who had not committed any crimes. And I think that it says so here, that the exchange should be carried out on the basis of the principle all-for-all, and also that it was prohibited to take any kind of financial remuneration for the exchanges. That would be it, as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, were these efforts genuine?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the government, yes. I think that this order was carried out to a considerable degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like you to have a look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you dealt with the matter, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question you said: "And the position was to carry out an exchange -- or rather, to first release all those civilians who had not participated in war operations ..." Where do I find that -- do I find that in this document specifically or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you answer my question? I was asking whether we find anywhere in the documents that you were presented with this specific point you mentioned, that is: "To first release all those civilians who had not participated in war operations."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the information provided by the commission that toward Krajina this provision is contained and there are three categories. The first one are the civilians who have to be released immediately; the second category are people who collected weapons for war operations; and the third category were people who were engaged in war operations. So this is an integral part of this decree, and I think that it's contained in the materials. That provision, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I did not find it in the materials you presented to the witness at this moment, but of course reading through it very quickly, I might have missed something. I take it you will draw your attention to it if it's found somewhere. General instruction: Release all civilians that had not been involved in war operations. Mr. Josse, for reasons unknown to you, I'd like to have an earlier break. Could you find a moment within the next two or three minutes to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now would be as good as any. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then we will have an early break today at this moment. Mr. Lakic, we'll have a break for -- until five minutes past 4.00, and I hope to be able to re-start at that time. I could be a couple of minutes late.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What's -- I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, it's the matter of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. I suggest that we do that first after the break, if that is suitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I hope Mr. Stewart is going to be here. I'd invite -- he's -- he's on his way, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Has that -- because there's an urgent matter I'd like to deal with at this very moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course. Perhaps Your Honour should rise and we'll start that out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll re-start most likely at five minutes past 4.00, and we'll then first give an opportunity to Mr. Krajisnik, so the witness could then wait outside the courtroom until he's called in again. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for the late start, but it was not totally unexpected. Mr. Krajisnik, you asked whether you could address the Court. Could that be done in open session or would you rather do that in private or closed session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see you nodding, I take it then that you agree then with open session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to thank the Trial Chamber for allowing me to address them. I will try to be as brief as possible, not to take up your time. There are two reasons. One is my health condition, which is closely linked to this trial. In actual fact, I would first of all like to say to you, Your Honours, I am a man who respects people; I respect you, too. If I say something, please do not understand that as lack of respect for the Court, least of all lack of respect for you as individuals. But I would like to say something in relation to these two problems. You know that my lawyer familiarised you with the situation, and the doctors have provided their report as well. In the meantime, my condition has been -- improved and I was happy. But now, in fact, my condition is the same -- or rather, it's come back. I've started sweating during the night again, changing my clothes, that's an enormous problem. And I'm going to say why I think I feel that way. I am worried about the way this trial is progressing. You decided - probably rightly so - that I should not defend myself. I am just asking for a fair trial. I don't think I would be affected in any way if that were so. Now, why am I affected this badly? What's the problem? You know that the main problem of the Defence is time. Every moment should be used for preparing the Defence, especially my own testimony. Yesterday there was a culmination. Please don't mind my saying so, but Mr. Radojko's testimony was a culmination. I saw that it's the Prosecutor who gets our free time. I'll explain what I mean. For the first time, my counsel and I saw Radojko here when he came here and we had a meeting with him for one hour, whereas the gentlemen of the Prosecution had preparations with him for a few days -- or rather, an interview. And they prepared him for testifying here, then they had Brdjanin here. Now when my counsel finished, having made a maximum effort to examine Mr. Radojko, then the esteemed Mr. Tieger practically got unlimited time to examine the witness on a countless number of documents. Every time I get this many documents, as I've shown you. I continue to live in archives, among archives, and instead of using this free time for preparing my testimony -- well, also, we're waiting to see here now whether the witness will make a mistake and establish some link with Pale. I never saw him and I never saw his president. I'm very worried. This is one of the questions that worries me. It's not only now. All our witnesses got heaps of documents from the Prosecutors and only a few documents from our lawyers because they cannot prepare properly. I do not want to have any deferral of trial; I want this trial to be over as soon as possible. But I don't think it's right to be placed in an unfair position. The Prosecutor should have the same amount of time that we did. Remember how many times you interrupted us when we were questioning our witnesses. So that's the first question. The second question that worries me is our number of witnesses. 500 witnesses were interviewed. Mr. Stewart and our team -- well, maybe I'll exaggerate, but for a month we only made lists rather than prepare, how to reduce this to 20 witnesses. Your Honours, the truth here cannot be established only through the testimony of Momcilo Krajisnik, but through a number of witnesses. Somebody can say that Momcilo Krajisnik is partial. What particularly surprised me was that Mr. Stewart said that he would give up on the expert witness. I talked to him after that, asking him why he did that. Quite simply, he didn't have time and he also told me there is no money for that. So these witnesses would not be all that useful, then I just put a logical question. Why were they useful for the Prosecution? Why did they call six expert witnesses? Did they just waste their money or are expert witnesses useless? I'm sure that Mr. Stewart made a maximum effort, but I think it's a question of money and time. I'm saying all of this, Your Honours, for the benefit of the transcript, for history. I was a yardstick for a man who had good, solid nerves and was of sound health. Nowadays, I work until 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning so that we'd have enough time to agree on everything. And, quite simply, I see that we have to - well, please don't mind my saying so - but we have to find any kind of witnesses in order to get somebody in here because many of our witnesses were simply frightened. For those who have already testified, rumour has it now that they will be punished in some way, and some of them have already had their houses searched over there. So please don't mind what I'm saying, but I want to say that I'm glad you protect witnesses. Witnesses should be protected and nothing bad should be said about witnesses, but this witness who said that I fought with a man and took money away, well, you know, you'd have to say: Well, this person is a person, too. Let's check this out. Not only whether somebody took the money. All of this has an affect on a person. That's why I'm asking you and I'm addressing you, Mr. President of the Trial Chamber, and also Judge Canivell, please just give me a fair trial. In the depth of my heart I feel that it is not fair for the Prosecution to call 150 or so witnesses, whereas we barely have 20. And these people have such a lot of trouble bringing them in. So my health only gets worse on account of that, too. So, please, put us on a footing of equality, the Defence counsel and the Prosecution. Help us call two or three expert witnesses at least so that they would reply to the witnesses called by the Prosecution, so that I do not sweat at night during these countless nights in those archives. Please, for the sake of your own ethics, let me have a fair trial. I am happy that all of you will be examining me. Question me for ten years if you want, about anything, but Momcilo Krajisnik cannot replace witnesses who are here and who should be here. You've seen this man. He's afraid, and you don't know what happens to these people. I'm not going to talk about these cases from the court, generally speaking, and also the things that happened in prison. I'm now asking you only in my own name. Please, give me a fair trial. I'm sorry if I wasn't clear enough. If something was not clear, I'm prepared to explain, and I really appreciate the fact that you didn't interrupt me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. I'll not be able to deal with all the matters you've raised before I have consulted with my colleagues. One thing is two -- you may remain seated. There's no reason to stand, but you certainly raised clearly the health issue. You said where it improved it's now become worse again. We'll consider how to respond to that. Second, you have clearly expressed your concerns about time and facilities for the Defence. Of course that is an issue that has been discussed many, many times here, but that's not reason not to again discuss it thoroughly among ourselves after having given an opportunity to the Prosecution to also give their view on the matter. Finally, where you said you are insisting on receiving a fair trial, you brought that with - may I say - an almost desperate matter, calling upon us not to deprive you from a fair trial. We'll certainly consider that again. It's not the first time we'll consider it. It's often on our mind and it's often a subject in our discussions. Finally, you said that you are not raising certain matters also that happened in the Detention Unit recently. Without going into it, of course this Chamber is aware that it has an impact on everyone who is detained in the United Nations Detention Unit. Even without discussing it, even where you do not raise it, please be convinced that it's not something that we would not -- we would not be aware of. I mean, every human being would be aware of that. We'll take some more time to read again what you said, after having carefully listened to it, and then we'll come back on the matter. I can't say you -- tell you exactly when. Mr. Tieger, is there, at this moment, a need to give a response or would you rather first think it over, whether you would respond to Mr. Krajisnik's observations? Or would you say: Let the Chamber consider it as it deems fit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would be more than happy, and perhaps it's more prudent to reserve a response and consider whether any particular matters, or the matter more generally, will be assisted by any additional contributions from the Prosecution. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- rather than take up time at this point, I'd like to consider it and get back to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear, then, from you, I take it, somewhere in the beginning of next week whether there's any specific point on which you'd like to respond, and we'll further then consider the matter. Then if there's -- I was about to say if there's no other procedural issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Only this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My position is exactly the same as Mr. Tieger's, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a matter meriting consideration before we return to it. But just, with respect, to remind Your Honour that when Mr. Krajisnik says something and the Prosecution are invited to respond, Mr. Krajisnik is represented by counsel so that when the matter comes to be fully considered, Mr. Krajisnik's counsel have every bit then as much a role in the matter, certainly as prosecuting counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should have given you an opportunity. At the same time, I'm not seeking at any moment a situation where you would have to express not to fully or entirely support what Mr. Krajisnik said. I did understand that Mr. Krajisnik has consulted with you before making this statement. That's at least the impression I gained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We met, Your Honour, during the break. But, Your Honour, my position would have been this, exactly the same, in this respect, as Mr. Tieger's. It requires thinking about before anything further is being said. I don't wish to say anything this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's give it at least the weekend for further consideration and reflection. Yes. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Lakic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, you had to wait for quite some time. We would have wished to have you back earlier, but other matters asked our attention meanwhile. Mr. Josse will now continue his examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like you to have a look at the minutes of a closed session of the government held on the 19th of August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is the B/C/S version, and the English version to go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that P583, tab 38, I take it? 47th Session of government, 19th of August, 1992. And a -- well, we have to compare that also with P583, tab 91, because there seem to be two numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, there were two sessions that day I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can confirm that's the correct exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about number 1 which deals with captives, collective centres, investigation centres; and number 2 deals with accommodation, the military camp in Manjaca, prisoners of war. What was the government trying to achieve at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I -- I'm going to give another version of this to the witness. The one he's got is -- if Madam Usher could give him that, please. The one he was given had something printed on the reverse side which could only confuse. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What can you tell us about this, Mr. Lakic, if anything? If you don't remember, say so.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This report was put together based on a report by the commission which visited the centres for detainees in the western part of Republika Srpska. The essence of the conclusion made by the government here is that conditions related to accommodation should be improved concerning the detainees in the aforementioned centres; then, to create better conditions; to provide food; to provide security of the aforementioned facilities by the Ministry of Defence and of the Interior; and that the security of the facilities be transferred within the competency of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look, please, now at -- sorry, Mr. Lakic, had you finished?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can clearly see in the document as to how far you got with the question, that is, I wanted to say that the issue of Trnopolje should be dealt with as soon as possible and that the Ministry of Defence and of the Interior put into force regulation on the condition -- conditions prevailing in such detention centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was the state of knowledge at the time in relation to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report was not a very optimistic one; it was realistic in its essence, stating that the conditions should be improved because the detainees had to sleep on the ground in large rooms where they were all placed together. And I believe the only thing they had at their disposal were mattresses, if that's what they're called.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look, please, at tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This, I understand, is P583, tab 92, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How does this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and for the previous document I gave two numbers. I think the first one I gave was the minutes of the 47th Session which was not a closed session, and we dealt, as a matter of fact, with 5 -- 583, tab 91, which is the minutes of a closed session of the government on the 19th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The report that you now have in front of you, Mr. Lakic, that's dated the 22nd of August -- it was received the 22nd of August. The report itself is undated. How does that fit in to the minutes we have just looked at?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same person made the minutes in the eastern part of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, when you say "the same person made the minutes in the eastern part of Herzegovina," what do you mean by --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A member of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "minutes"?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is a separate report, is it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why was the session on the 19th of August a closed session?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whose decision was it to hold that session privately?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prime Minister was the one who always decided whether a session would be an open or a closed one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've looked, both before and after the break, at a couple of reports, some government minutes. Beyond what's contained in those reports, did you have any personal knowledge of what was happening at these various places of detention and in relation to people who were being detained?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might assist with the exhibit number for tab 8. It's P583, tab 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think I'd -- I think I'd mentioned that already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what my recollection is as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to move on to a different topic, please, Mr. Lakic. What did you understand in 1992 by the expression "expanded Presidency"?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the Presidency, the members of which were Mrs. Biljana Plavsic and Mr. Nikola Koljevic. When they held sessions, during such sessions the Prime Minister, the president of the Assembly, as well as the ministers who had to report on their respective issues were allowed to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was there a -- an expanded Presidency, as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because there were only two members to the Presidency according to the constitution. Later on a constitutional law was put into force appointing a third member of the Presidency, that being Mr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Djeric ever suggest to you that he was a member of an expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Please have a look at the minutes of the 23rd of May government session. It's item number 3 that I would like you to look at.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What did you understand that entry in the minutes to mean?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was war going on, but that is to be distinguished from the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was a state of war ever declared?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: By the end of 1995? Is what --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was it declared before that date?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have made a mistake, but it was certainly somewhere during 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd also like you to have a look at the minutes of the 31st of May, item number 1. Do these constitutional amendments help you on the issue of the expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It does not concern itself with the expanded Presidency of the RS but, rather, with the expanded Presidencies of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Put the document down for a moment. There was a war going on in Bosnia, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why wasn't a state of war declared by the government of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government had analysed the general situation and the developments during the war and was of the position that there was no need to declare a state of war. As the basis, they used the fact that once a state of war is declared, the functioning of all institutions in the RS are being put out of force, starting with the Assembly and the government, down to the municipalities. And the government was already in the process of undertaking the measures needed to organise the rule of law and the functioning of institutions, in particular the judiciary, the misdemeanour courts, and the criminal courts, that is. They functioned properly, hence the decision not to declare a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What would have been the effect on the government and administration of the Republika Srpska had a state of war been declared?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By having declared a state of war, only the expanded Presidency would have remained; everything else would not -- could not function.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In terms of functions, what was communications like between the government and municipalities? I know that's a very general question. If you can answer it in a general sense, do so; if you can't, say so.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government tasked individual ministers to visit Assemblies in the territories where they could go and the territories that they could reach those Assemblies and to keep them informed. But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, go on, Mr. Lakic.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communication was very difficult at the time. There were no links established. The territory was split in different parts and it was difficult to reach certain municipalities and people went the round-about way quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Krajisnik a member of an expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Krajisnik a member of the government?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik play any part in the government?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik did not play any part in the government. He exclusively worked with the functioning of the Assembly of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And beyond the functioning of the Assembly of the RS, where did his power lie?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps within the Serb Democratic Party, although it was separate from state functions, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he would also receive people coming in from the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why do you use the word "perhaps"?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was at Jahorina, and Mr. Krajisnik was in Kikinda. And the distance between the two is about 30 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Krajisnik, as far as you were aware, a popular figure in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. But his popularity was due to the fact that he was a good professional, a persistent person, and that he did good work as the Assembly president, prior to the war and during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik have the power to punish individuals?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because all the decisions were made by the Assembly. Mr. Krajisnik was the speaker of the Assembly, without any competences in particular. And I never heard and I never learned of him anyone -- punishing anyone ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of Mr. Krajisnik encouraging or endorsing war crimes?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the government that you were the chief civil servant of, did that have a plan to ethnically cleanse Muslims from large parts of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was that anything that was discussed, either at meetings, behind closed doors, or in any sense at all by the government or its members?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it wasn't discussed during any of the meetings or either during, be it the open or the closed, sessions of the government. The ethnic cleansing of territory was never discussed, at least not the territories that were under the governmental control.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Same question in relation to the Presidency. Did you ever get the impression that it was a policy of the Presidency to ethnically cleanse large parts of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't communicate with the Presidency at all, meaning I wasn't present during their sessions. As regards their position, the -- that was never discussed with the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Tieger, could you start with the cross-examination of Mr. Lakic? I take it that we'll have a break at approximately -- in approximately 15 minutes -- oh, Mr. Margetts, I'm addressing Mr. Tieger and I should have addressed you, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You say that we'll have a break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After approximately 15 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number of matters that were raised in that examination that were not part of the 65 ter, and it's our submission that we'll need time to consider those matters and we'd ask for a break of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: At this moment and continuing for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so we then re-start at quarter to 6.00? Is that -- ten minutes to 6.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Ten minutes to 6.00, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
